turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the eleventh of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things up top. The war over the Strait of Hormuz just found a second strait to sit on — and the oil price noticed.
In Singapore, the prime minister's pay goes up sixty-four per cent — the same week the cost-of-living cheques land. [wry] The timing writes its own comment section.
And, later, the grown men thinning their paints. [deadpan] It's a real hobby. It's enormous.
[amused] I have so many questions about that one.
[warmly] You'll get answers, I promise. But start with the war.
For weeks this has been the Strait of Hormuz — the tanker war, the shooting war. On Wednesday it widened. Yemen's Houthis captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and started pushing toward Bab el-Mandeb.
Translate that for me. Why does a second strait matter?
Because it's the other oil gate. Hormuz is the way out of the Gulf; Bab el-Mandeb is the way into the Suez trade. Threaten both, and you're squeezing the same barrel from two directions.
[thoughtful] So one chokepoint was the whole story, and now there are two.

And Hormuz is still hot. Fresh strikes on southern Iran on Thursday; Iran says it damaged jets at a base in Jordan — Washington disputes that. The price did the talking. Brent crude ran past a hundred and four dollars a barrel.
Which is a lot. Put it in scale for me.
Iran's blockade now chokes roughly a fifth of world oil supply. That's about twice the disruption of the nineteen-seventies shock.
[exhales] Twice the seventies. Okay.

We laid the viewpoints side by side, as always. Washington frames a dangerous new phase driven by Iran, and reports no American casualties. Tehran calls it a strategic defeat of the United States. Doha — Al Jazeera — leads on the widening and the risk to Saudi crude.
And is anyone talking their way out of this?
Not visibly. President Trump waved the June ceasefire away — quote, not worth the paper it's written on — and said the war would end after the election.
That's grim. [pause] Is there a case that this calms down fast?

There is, and it's the sceptic's case. The market keeps fading these spikes. Every time talks look possible, Brent sells off. Goldman's baseline had actually been cut toward eighty dollars on an expected deal.
So the crowd is betting on calm even while the missiles fly.

The prediction markets put a ceasefire holding to month-end at about seventy-seven per cent. The rebuttal is uncomfortable, though — most of the world's spare oil capacity sits inside the very Gulf that's now under fire.
[thoughtful] Right. The insurance is in the burning building.

Two quick ones elsewhere. Ukraine's three-day pause on strikes expired Monday; Russia hit Kyiv within hours. And Nepal's young government — a thirty-five-year-old former rapper as prime minister — is meeting its first real test, a flood, a year after the protests that put it in power.
Okay. Follow the oil into the money, because I know it goes somewhere.
It goes straight to the central banks — and this is the money block. One oil shock, three banks tightening at once.
Tightening — meaning raising rates. Into a war. That feels backwards.

It's the stagflation trap. Expensive oil pushes inflation up even as growth slows, and a central bank only has the one lever — so it has to choose which problem to make worse. On Wednesday the European Central Bank raised its deposit rate a quarter-point, to two and a half per cent. Christine Lagarde called it a no-brainer, and warned inflation would stay above target for an extended period.
And ours — the Fed?

Meeting next week, and the market now prices about a seventy per cent chance it hikes too. The US ten-year Treasury yield hit four point eight four per cent — its highest since two thousand and seven.
[gasps] Two thousand and seven. That's before the last crisis.

[thoughtful] Here's the part that matters for a portfolio. Stocks and bonds are falling together. The government bond that's supposed to cushion a stock drop isn't cushioning anything this cycle — the correlation has turned the wrong way.
So the classic sixty-forty — the safety blanket — has a hole in it.

For now, yes. Gold is caught two ways — near a record on war demand, but capped by those rising real yields; it fell almost two per cent on the day. Bitcoin is heavy, near seventy-nine thousand dollars, trading like a risk asset, not a haven.
And the honest caveat?
This is market explanation, not advice — and it can reverse on one ceasefire headline. The August inflation print lands tonight, our time. We're holding it until it's real.
Now bring it home. The pay row.
Parliament spent Thursday on the political salary rise. And the striking thing was the agreement. The Workers' Party backed the increase.
[curious] The opposition backed it? So what was the fight about?

Disclosure. Pritam Singh said yes to the rise, given inflation — then pressed for the ministers' total pay to be published, not just the headline benchmark. There was no vote. It was, in form, symbolic.
And the numbers everyone's actually chewing on?

The prime minister's pay climbs sixty-four per cent, to three point six million dollars. The median full-time wage in Singapore is five thousand seven hundred and seventy-five a month. The cheques cleared two days earlier.
[sighs] Yeah. The optics do the rest.

The sceptic's line: even the opposition agrees pay should rise, so the real argument is what the public gets to see, next to a same-week relief payout. That's the unfinished business. And the haze tipped into unhealthy on Thursday before the rain pulled it back.
Good. Take me to the machines. Chips and gear.
The big one: DeepSeek, China's most talked-about A-I lab, is filing to list in Shanghai — and agreeing, for the first time, to open its books.
Meaning what, concretely?

A listing forces audited accounts, a full prospectus, and a disclosure of how much computing hardware it actually commands. For a company that's been a black box, that's the real news. It's raising money at around seventy-five billion US dollars, and the whole thing lands two weeks before Xi Jinping visits.
[skeptical] And the catch? There's always a catch.

Wedbush's Dan Ives supplies it. No big American company, he says, is going to build its A-I on a Chinese start-up. So the listing monetises a domestic story — not the Western market that valuation might imply.
You had something for my home lab, too.
A call-back, actually. That open model we flagged a couple of weeks ago — G-L-M five-three Flash — has quietly become the most-used open model online, roughly twice DeepSeek's usage at launch.
[amused] The one that doesn't fit any normal computer.

The very one — three hundred and twenty billion parameters. So the thing to actually run is its little brother, G-L-M four-seven Flash. Thirty billion, fits one card, and it's new. Memory prices are climbing, so a model that fits one card is the sensible endgame right now.
And on the wrist? Because I know you've got a watch.
The Apple Watch Ultra Four. Seven hundred and ninety-nine dollars, in stores next Thursday. Faster chip, denser health sensing, a longer battery.
You said that flatly. What are you not saying?

[deadpan] It's the same body as last year's Ultra Three. Identical case. And the marquee feature is a wrist assistant. When Tom's Guide polled its readers, out of three hundred and sixty-eight people, exactly eleven said they wanted A-I on the wrist.
[laughs] Eleven. Out of three hundred and sixty-eight.
They wanted battery. They got an assistant. For a buy-once reader, the honest question is whether a discounted Ultra Three does the same job.
Okay — The Atelier. This is our buy-it-once desk, and today it's jeans. Convince me raw denim is worth a lecture.

Because most of what you're told is marketing, and the mechanism isn't. Selvedge is just the clean, self-finished edge a narrow shuttle loom leaves. Rope-dyed indigo only coats the surface of the yarn, leaving a white core — and that white core is the entire engine of the fades people chase.
So the fading isn't damage. It's the design.

It's the sport — the entire point. There's a contest, the Indigo Invitational: you wear one pair, unwashed, for three hundred and sixty-five days, and the best fade wins. Fifteen hundred people entered the last one.
[gasps] A whole year? No wash?

A whole year. [chuckles] The community has opinions about hygiene, and so do I. But here's the white-label truth, which is this desk's beat: one mill, Kaihara, weaves for Levi's and Uniqlo and half the Japanese market. Uniqlo's Kaihara selvedge is the same mill at a fraction of the price.
And for a hot, wet Singapore?

Go lighter — twelve to fourteen ounces — and sanforized, so you skip the shrink gamble. The twenty-one-ounce heavyweight is a beautiful enthusiast object, not a daily driver in thirty degrees and full humidity. And a fashion-house pair over a thousand dollars is buying you a logo, not better cloth — above about three hundred, you're mostly paying for a name.
[warmly] Alright. I've been waiting for this one.
I know you have.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this.
[laughs] Today it's tabletop miniature painting. Warhammer figures, D-and-D minis, the little soldiers. And apparently it's massive?
Massive. The company at the centre, Games Workshop, just posted record half-year revenue — three hundred and thirty-two million pounds. The whole market is headed past seven billion dollars.
What's the first rule? Every hobby has a first rule.
[amused] Thin your paints. It's the reflexive answer to every beginner on the forums. Paint straight from the pot and you drown the detail.
So what pulled all these people in?

A revolution in the paint itself. One-coat paints — Contrast, Speedpaint — that shade and base a model in a single pass. They collapsed the skill floor. A beginner can finish something that looks good in an afternoon.
And then the spending starts.
[wry] Then the spending starts. One brand relaunched its range to two hundred and sixteen colours — more than the market leader. You need about fifteen.
[laughs] Two hundred and sixteen. You need fifteen.

And the brushes are the trap. The famous kolinsky sable, the Winsor and Newton Series Seven, runs about forty-two dollars. The enthusiasts' pick — a Rosemary and Company brush at a fraction of that — many say holds paint better and lasts longer.
So the expensive one doesn't make you better.

The tools don't paint the model. Skill does — reviewers rate the cheaper brush equal or better. There's a whole economy above it, mind you — commission painters who'll do a tabletop army for a few dollars a figure, or a display centrepiece that's twenty to forty hours of work, priced like the small atelier it really is.
Any drama? I love a hobby with drama.

[chuckles] Games Workshop banned generative A-I from its work and its competitions — to respect its human artists. The painters cheered. And the community's honest confession has a name: the pile of shame.
The pile of shame?
The stash of unpainted models that grows faster than anyone can paint it. [warmly] Every hobbyist owns one, and every hobbyist laughs about it.
[laughs] I feel seen, and I don't even do this.
Let's do culture and the body, quickly. Venice.
The film festival. Who won?

Nobody yet — the Golden Lion is handed out Saturday, the day after we print. What's loud are two premieres whose applause is running ahead of their reviews. A Florian Zeller film, Bunker, got about sixteen minutes of ovation; a McDonagh film, Wild Horse Nine, about thirteen.
An ovation isn't a verdict, though.

[thoughtful] It's a room's mood, not a verdict — the reviews are already arguing with the applause. And a music note for the mid-forties shelf: Bloc Party released a new album today, produced by Trevor Horn. A break-up told in fourteen songs, first glance to last goodbye.
Oof. That's a specific kind of evening.

One watch, fast: Tudor revived the North Flag as a proper travel G-M-T with a Master Chronometer stamp, at five thousand five hundred and twenty-five dollars. The movement earns it; the old, angular case is the argument.
And the family desk? My people with kids are listening.
The newest big screen-time study — fifty thousand children — points somewhere useful. The harm from heavy screens runs mostly through what they displace: lost sleep and lost exercise.
[thoughtful] So it's not the phone, exactly.

It's the bedtime it eats and the afternoon it replaces — and those are the two things a parent can actually control. During exam season here, that's the whole game: charge the phone outside the bedroom, and protect one hour outdoors, even in the week before the papers. General guidance, not medical advice.
And keeping ourselves alive — Fitness?
A tidy meta-analysis on creatine after sixty. It works — real gains in the legs and in lean mass — but only alongside the lifting. The powder builds nothing on its own.
[wry] The barbell does the work. The tub just helps.

And on the calendar: the Singapore Grand Prix, the ninth to the eleventh of October, with the city's first-ever Sprint weekend, and The Killers and Lana Del Rey on the Padang stages. Snow City closes for good on the thirtieth of September, after twenty-six years — a genuine last outing for a twelve-year-old. And if you're planning Japan, the Kyushu sumo tickets open on the nineteenth, and they sell out in hours.
Good. Land us on the long read. Slow it down.

[warmly] This one I loved. Thailand. There's a folk opera from the poor northeast called mor lam — sung poetry over a bamboo mouth-organ, a troupe of forty playing a village field until two in the morning.
[curious] And that's… trending?

[excited] It's become the biggest concert format in the country. Six billion baht, reaching around twenty million people a year. And the national brands have noticed — the top energy drink now gives away gold at the shows.
Gold. At a village concert.

[drawn out] Gold. There are patrons — older women, mostly — who'll shower a favourite singer with up to fifty thousand baht in a single night. The industry has coined a word for chasing this audience: upcountry entertainment.
So why does it matter beyond Thailand?

Because the growth story everyone tells is about Bangkok's malls. This is the counter-story: the spending is moving to the poorest region — a place the capital spent a century looking down on. The parallel is American country music. Regional, working-class, dismissed as lowbrow, then industrialised with beer sponsorship and a politics of its own.
[thoughtful] And the shadow on it?

It's real but thin. The money is largely remitted home by the young people who had to leave to earn it. A boom financed by the people who aren't there. [pause] When the Financial Times writes this up in three weeks, remember which desk told you first.
[warmly] That's the whole reason to read ahead.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
